courses.title: The 13th Grade
courses.description: Working on your mindset, your money, and dealing with life's big calls. 24 bite-size units, each paired with a chapter of the book.

units.title: Mindset Hacks
units.blurb: Habits, discipline, and talking to yourself like a coach instead of a critic.
units.action: Tonight, pick one habit, shrink it to a two-minute version, and anchor it to something you already do every day ("after dinner, I open the notebook"). Then write down the emergency version, the one-line move you'll make on the day everything falls apart.
asks: According to the unit, where does the critic voice actually come from?
You blew a presentation. Which line passes the coach test?
Which of these is a standard rather than a verdict?
Why do tiny habits work, according to the unit?
You planned to review flashcards nightly and missed Tuesday completely. What matters most now?
What should the 66-day figure change about how you plan a new habit?

units.title: The Comparison Trap
units.blurb: Instagram is not a benchmark. Building your own scoreboard.
units.action: Mute three accounts that reliably make you feel behind, and write this week's three-line scoreboard: what moved that YOU control.
asks: Why is comparing yourself to social media rigged from the start?
The healthy replacement for comparing to strangers is…
Envy at someone's post is most useful as…
What's the point of muting instead of doom-scrolling past accounts that sting?

units.title: First Principles Thinking
units.blurb: Strip a problem down to what's actually true, then rebuild from there.
units.action: Take one recurring expense or one inherited rule you follow, and run the two-question drill on paper. Keep it or replace it, on purpose.
asks: First principles thinking means…
"You need a car." The first-principles move is:
A family expectation like "be a doctor or engineer" decompresses to…
When should you NOT run the first-principles drill?

units.title: Habit Loops
units.blurb: Cue, routine, reward: wiring the boring stuff to run on autopilot.
units.action: Pick one bad loop. Name its cue, routine, and reward on paper, then add 20 seconds of friction to the routine or swap it while keeping the cue and reward.
asks: The three parts of every habit loop:
Why do people with "great discipline" mostly succeed?
You scroll in bed every night and hate it. The highest-payoff fix:
Breaking a bad habit usually works best by…

units.title: Emotional Intelligence 101
units.blurb: Reading the room, naming the feeling, responding instead of reacting.
units.action: Next time something spikes you this week, take the one breath and name the feeling precisely: out loud if you can, on paper if you can't. Notice what changes.
asks: "Name it to tame it" works because…
The most useful thing to do in the gap between trigger and response:
Someone who's usually chatty goes quiet in a meeting. The EQ read:
"Do whatever you want" from a partner or parent usually means…

units.title: Boundaries
units.blurb: Saying no without burning bridges: at work, at home, in the group chat.
units.action: Identify one standing yes you regret: a task, a group chat, a recurring favor. This week, deliver the no + alternative, calmly, once.
asks: Saying yes when you mean no is usually…
The "broken record" technique:
In a family where a flat no reads as disrespect, the move is:
A boundary you announce but never enforce is…

units.title: Rejection Practice
units.blurb: Getting told no on purpose until it stops being scary.
units.action: Make one small ask today that you expect to be denied. The fee waiver is the classic. Whatever the answer, notice the two seconds and what comes after.
asks: What shapes most lives more than rejection itself?
The goal of deliberately collecting small nos is…
You get a no. The highest-value follow-up is…
"Asking feels like imposing." The reframe is:

units.title: Purpose, Roughly
units.blurb: You don't need a calling. You need a direction and a next step.
units.action: Answer the four compass questions on paper, write one rough heading from them, and schedule the first three-hour block this week.
asks: Why does "find your passion" mostly produce paralysis?
A rough heading plus motion beats a perfect plan because…
Passion usually arrives…
What is this year's anger or heartbreak useful for?

units.title: Money 101
units.blurb: Budgeting that doesn't feel like punishment. Where your paycheck actually goes.
units.action: Find your real monthly take-home number, then set up one automatic transfer to savings on payday. Even $25 counts. The habit matters more than the amount.
asks: Your offer letter says $60,000. Why is your monthly budget NOT based on $5,000?
In the 50/30/20 split, the 20 goes to…
Your needs eat 65% of take-home because your city is expensive. What's the right read?
Why automate savings on payday?

units.title: Tax Season, Decoded
units.blurb: W-2? 1099? Refund? Plain English, before April ruins your month.
units.action: Find last year's tax documents (or your W-4 from your current job) and check one thing: how much is being withheld per paycheck. If you have any 1099 income this year, open a separate account today and move 25–30% of it there.
asks: You made $2,000 on a freelance project (1099). What's the move?
A big tax refund means…
What does the standard deduction do?
You earn $55k at a W-2 job and have simple taxes. What should filing cost you?

units.title: Credit Glow-Up
units.blurb: From "no score" to "approved" without falling for a single trap.
units.action: Check your credit score for free this week (your bank app almost certainly shows it). No score yet? Look up one secured or student card and read its terms. Just read, no application needed.
asks: The single biggest factor in your credit score is…
"You need to carry a balance to build credit" is…
Your limit is $1,000. For a great utilization number, keep the reported balance under…
Why keep your first credit card open even after you get better ones?

units.title: Invest, Eventually
units.blurb: 401(k)s and index funds for people with fifty bucks and a dream.
units.action: Log into your payroll portal and check two things: are you getting the full employer match, and what fund your money is actually in. No job benefits yet? Look up one S&P 500 index fund and note its expense ratio.
asks: Your employer matches 401(k) contributions up to 4% of salary. Not contributing means…
Why do index funds beat stock-picking for normal people?
You have credit card debt at 22% APR and $300 spare each month (after getting the full 401(k) match). What's the move?
The market drops 20% two years into your plan. The pre-written move is…

units.title: Paychecks & Benefits
units.blurb: The 401(k) match, the HSA, the insurance elections: the form nobody explains.
units.action: Open your benefits portal this week and answer three questions: am I getting the full match, which health plan am I on and why, and is there an HSA or education budget I'm ignoring?
asks: The HSA's superpower is…
The FSA differs from the HSA how?
How do you honestly compare two health plans?
The most common benefits mistake:

units.title: Debt, Strategically
units.blurb: Student loans, car notes, and the order to pay them down in.
units.action: Make the one-page list tonight: every balance, rate, and minimum. Sort by rate. Circle the fire, pick avalanche or snowball, and point this month's spare dollars at one target.
asks: The first strategic move against debt is…
Avalanche vs snowball. The honest answer for most people:
You have a 4.5% student loan and a 24% card. Spare dollars go…
"Can you lower my APR?" is…

units.title: Emergency Funds
units.blurb: Why three months of rent in a boring account beats any hot tip.
units.action: Open a high-yield savings account this week (15 minutes) and automate the first transfer for the day after payday, even $50. Name the account something that talks back.
asks: The emergency fund's actual job is…
"Three months of expenses" means…
Why keep it in an HYSA instead of index funds?
You spent $800 from the fund on an urgent car repair. This means…

units.title: Negotiation
units.blurb: Asking for more (salary, rent, bills) without your voice shaking.
units.action: Pick your ugliest recurring bill and make the retention call this week: competitor offer cited, one number anchored, one silence survived. Report the savings to someone.
asks: Why does anchoring with a number and a reason beat "can you do better?"
The magic word when calling about a bill is…
Why decide your walk-away before the conversation?
"Haggling is embarrassing." The reframe:

units.title: The Big Calls
units.blurb: Career moves, new cities, big relationships: how to actually think them through.
units.action: Write down one real decision you've been circling. Sort it (two-way or one-way door), run 10/10/10 and the friend test on paper, and give yourself a decision deadline: date and time.
asks: First move on any big decision?
The 10/10/10 lens asks…
Why does the friend test work?
You have 70% of the information on a reversible call. The move is…

units.title: First Apartments
units.blurb: Leases, deposits, roommates: what to read before you sign.
units.action: Moving soon or not, compute your real monthly housing number today: current place or target place, all-in. Check it against 30% of take-home and see what the gap is funding or costing.
asks: The "real monthly number" for a $1,400 apartment is…
The single best protector of your security deposit:
Why visit the apartment at night before signing?
The roommate conversation that matters most BEFORE move-in:

units.title: Career Moves
units.blurb: When to stay, when to jump, and how to tell the difference.
units.action: Run the four-question audit on paper for your current (or most recent) year, and do the one-hour market check on your title. Two numbers and four colors: that's your career dashboard.
asks: The four yearly audit questions:
"Auditing" your employer yearly is…
The audit fails but you like the company. First moves:
Why update your resume every six months even when happy?

units.title: New Cities
units.blurb: Moving somewhere you know nobody: the checklist and the math.
units.action: Pick a city you've wondered about and run budget one on paper tonight: real listings, tax difference, move cost, runway number. Even if you never go, now the daydream has a price tag.
asks: A +$14k offer in a city where rent is +$700/month is…
The runway rule for landing in a new city:
The loneliness budget is best spent on…
Leaving parents who rely on you is…

units.title: Big Relationships
units.blurb: Money talks, moving in, and the conversations that decide everything.
units.action: Partnered or still evaluating, write the four threshold questions somewhere private and answer them for yourself first. You can't compare answers you haven't formed.
asks: The strongest researched predictor of relationship failure:
"Sliding vs deciding" refers to…
Which is a rough edge rather than a red flag?
Family involvement in choosing a partner means the framework…

units.title: Health & Insurance
units.blurb: Deductibles, premiums, networks: decoded before you need them.
units.action: Find your plan's five numbers this week (insurance app or HR portal): premium, deductible, copay, coinsurance, out-of-pocket max. Write them where future-you can find them in a waiting room.
asks: The out-of-pocket maximum is…
You're insured with a $2,000 deductible you haven't touched. A $150 doctor visit costs you…
The two-minute habit before planned procedures:
Skipping your annual physical to save money is…

units.title: Family Money Talks
units.blurb: Helping parents, taking help, and keeping all of it healthy.
units.action: If money flows between you and family in any direction: write the current reality down (amounts, frequency, terms, or the fog where terms should be), and pick ONE conversation from this unit to have this month.
asks: The sustainable structure for supporting parents:
Accepting a large money gift from parents. The key move:
The rule for lending to family:
Siblings splitting parent support unevenly. The fix:

units.title: The Ten-Year View
units.blurb: Zooming out: decisions that compound, and the ones that don't matter.
units.action: Write the ten-year letter tonight: one page, an ordinary Tuesday, specific. Then install one default it requires (an automation, a weekly block, a standing call) before the week ends.
asks: The core insight of the ten-year view:
Which list is "compounds FOR you"?
Most people budget their anxiety backwards, meaning…
The graduation assignment is…

courses.title: The 14th Grade
courses.description: The deeper money course: negotiate what you earn, put it to work, and protect it from taxes, bad products, and scams. 12 units, plain English throughout.

units.title: Salary Negotiation
units.blurb: The script, the silence, and why the first number matters so much.
units.action: Write your four sentences for your current job or next interview, with a real number in them. Say them out loud twice: the words need to have been in your mouth before the day they matter.
asks: Why does a higher starting salary matter beyond year one?
What actually gets offers pulled?
You said your number. The recruiter goes quiet. You should…
The recruiter says the base is truly fixed. Best response?

units.title: Job Offer Math
units.blurb: Base, bonus, equity, benefits: comparing offers on the full number.

units.title: Side Income
units.blurb: Turning a skill into a second paycheck without burning out.

units.title: Freelance Basics
units.blurb: Contracts, invoices, and getting paid on time, every time.

units.title: Index Funds, Actually Explained
units.blurb: What you own, what it costs, and why fees decide more than skill.
units.action: Open your 401(k) or brokerage portal and find two numbers: what fund your money is in, and its expense ratio. If it's cash or above 0.5%, you found this month's highest-value ten minutes.
asks: A target-date fund (e.g. Target 2065)…
Fund A charges 0.04%, Fund B charges 1%. Over 30 years on a retirement account, the difference is roughly…
The most expensive common 401(k) mistake is…
A fair expense ratio for a broad index fund is…

units.title: The Retirement Alphabet
units.blurb: 401(k), IRA, Roth, HSA: which bucket, in which order, and why.

units.title: Brokerage Basics
units.blurb: Opening an account, placing your first order, and the settings that matter.

units.title: Risk & Time
units.blurb: Why your age changes the answer, and what "risk tolerance" actually means.

units.title: Scam-Proof
units.blurb: The scripts scammers use on smart people, and the two-step habit that beats all of them.
units.action: Have the two-step conversation with one family member this week, parents first. Agree out loud: any call about money gets a hang-up and an official callback, no exceptions.
asks: "Your account is compromised. Read me the code we just texted so I can verify you." This is…
The two-step habit that defeats nearly every scam:
Caller ID shows your bank's real name and number. This means…
Authority + urgency + gift cards. How many of these does a real institution use?

units.title: Taxes, Level Two
units.blurb: Brackets, capital gains, and the moves that legally shrink the bill.

units.title: Insurance, Decoded
units.blurb: What to insure, what to skip, and how deductibles really work.

units.title: Beneficiaries & Wills
units.blurb: The one-page folder your family hopes you have.

courses.title: The 15th Grade
courses.description: Frameworks for the decisions that shape your decade: quitting, moving, buying, marrying, caring for parents. 12 units, no easy answers pretended, real ones worked through.

units.title: Quit or Stay
units.blurb: The four signals that say go, the two that say wait, and the exit done right.
units.action: Write the six-month list: what would need to be true for staying to be right. For each item, note whether you've actually asked for it. That page is your next move.
asks: Better than asking "should I quit?" is asking…
Your manager is the only bad part of an otherwise good job. The framework says…
Why interview while still employed?
You've asked twice for a raise with clear reasoning; silence both times. Leaving now is…

units.title: Career Pivots
units.blurb: Changing lanes without starting from zero: what transfers and what doesn't.

units.title: Grad School Math
units.blurb: When the degree pays for itself, and when it's an expensive pause button.

units.title: Starting Something
units.blurb: Side project to real business: the checkpoints that tell you to keep going.

units.title: Rent vs Buy
units.blurb: The five-year rule, the hidden costs, and why renting is often the smart move.
units.action: Run your city's numbers: your rent vs. the full monthly cost (mortgage + taxes + insurance + 1%/12 maintenance) of a place you'd actually buy. Then answer honestly: five-plus years, or not?
asks: The mortgage would equal your current rent. The honest cost comparison is…
Why does the five-year rule exist?
"Rent is throwing money away." What's rent actually buying?
Buying most clearly wins when…

units.title: Moving Math
units.blurb: New city, new country, new cost of living: the full comparison, not just salary.

units.title: Living With Parents
units.blurb: Moving back home with a plan: saving aggressively without losing momentum.

units.title: First Home Playbook
units.blurb: Down payments, mortgages, inspections: the process from search to keys.

units.title: Partner Money Talks
units.blurb: The five conversations to have before you combine anything.
units.action: Pick conversation one ("what did money feel like growing up?") and have it this week. It's the gentlest of the five and it makes the other four easier.
asks: When should you learn each other's real financial facts (income, debts, scores)?
One partner earns double. Why do proportional contributions usually beat 50/50?
"I send my parents money monthly and always will." This belongs…
Which is a red flag rather than a workable difference?

units.title: Wedding Math
units.blurb: Celebrating big without starting married life in debt, and handling family expectations.

units.title: The Kids Question
units.blurb: The real costs, the real timelines, and deciding on purpose instead of by default.

units.title: Aging Parents
units.blurb: Supporting the people who raised you: money, care, and boundaries that keep love intact.
